274.title: Hillel on the roof (Yoma 35b)
274.hook: too poor for the fee, young Hillel lay on the skylight in the snow to hear the lesson
274.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats Torah study as open to everyone, rich or poor, and the story of Hillel on the roof is often told to children and adults to show how much learning is worth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shammai's builder's rod, and the Talmud's lesson to be patient like Hillel. Your line was be patient like Hillel. Today, how Hillel himself learned.

Think of the last time you really wanted to be somewhere and couldn't afford it. A concert. A class. A trip your friends were taking. You stood outside it, in a way. Before Hillel was the great Hillel, he was a poor young man from Babylonia, working for tiny wages in Jerusalem. The best teachers in the city taught in a study house with a guard at the door and a fee to get in. One winter day he didn't have the fee. So what did he do?
screen: `OUTSIDE SOMETHING YOU WANTED.` → `A POOR YOUNG MAN IN JERUSALEM.` → `NO FEE TODAY.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Yoma. Every day Hillel worked and earned a small coin. Half went to the guard of the study house, where the teachers Shemaya and Avtalyon taught. Half fed his family. One day he earned nothing, and the guard wouldn't let him in. So Hillel climbed onto the roof and lay down by the skylight, to hear the words of the living God from their mouths. It was a Friday in the dead of winter, and snow began to fall. He stayed. The snow covered him. In the morning, Shemaya said to Avtalyon: my brother, every day this house is bright, and today it's dark. Is it cloudy? They looked up and saw the shape of a man in the skylight. They climbed up and found Hillel under a thick layer of snow. They brought him down, washed him, rubbed him with oil, and sat him by the fire, though it was Shabbat. This one, they said, is worth breaking the Sabbath for. Saving a life overrides Shabbat for anyone; the line is their way of saying how much they loved him. The Talmud tells the story for a reason. When poor people are asked why they didn't learn, it says, the answer comes back: were you poorer than Hillel? That's a hard question. But it isn't a scolding. It's an invitation. Learning finds a way in, even through the roof.

Now picture the skylight, one small way in anyway: a free library book, ten minutes before bed, a question to someone who knows. Hold that one way in.

275.title: Water wears stone (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 6)
275.hook: Akiva, an unlettered shepherd of forty, sees water carve a hole in rock
275.howItsDone: Akiva's stone is often retold in Jewish education to encourage adult beginners, and studying a little every day is a common Jewish practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shemaya and Avtalyon's study house, and young Hillel listening from the snowy roof. Your line was listen through the snow.

A well. A shepherd stops beside it and stares at one stone in its rim. There's a hole worn clean through it, smooth as the inside of a cup. By the story's telling, the shepherd is forty years old, and he has never learned a single letter. Not one. He's about to ask a simple question about that stone. And the answer will start him on the road to becoming Rabbi Akiva.
screen: `A STONE AT A WELL.` → `A SHEPHERD OF FORTY.` → `ONE SIMPLE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The story is in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early companion to Pirkei Avot. At the well, Akiva sees the hollowed stone and asks: who carved this? They tell him: the water that falls on it, every day, all the time. And they quote Job: "The waters wear the stones." Akiva reasons it out. If something soft like water can carve something hard like stone, then the words of Torah, strong as iron, can surely carve a way into my heart, which is only flesh and blood. So he goes to school. A grown man, with his little son, sitting with the children's teacher. He takes one end of the writing tablet, his son the other, and they learn the alphabet together. Alef, bet. Then Leviticus. Then the rest of the Torah. In time, the story says, he was teaching crowds. The water isn't a flood. It's drops. Nothing happens on the first day, or the hundredth. The stone looks exactly the same for a very long time. Then one day there's a hole. That's the picture Akiva carried: not talent, not a lightning bolt, but a small thing done every day for a long time. It's also why this path gives you one small lesson a day.

Picture that drop tomorrow, the day after, and a year of days, and let the stone wait.

276.title: Akiva and Rachel (Ketubot 62b–63a)
276.hook: his wife sends him to study for years; he tells his students that all they have is hers
276.howItsDone: The story of Akiva and Rachel is often retold in Jewish classes as a picture of a partnership built on learning, and of saying thank you in public.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Akiva, the shepherd of forty who saw a stone worn through by drops. Your line was learn the alphabet together. Today, the person who made his drops possible.

Watch the end of any awards show. Someone holds up a statue and thanks their spouse, their mom, the teacher who stayed late. Sometimes it's a line. Sometimes you can tell the person in the audience gave up years for this. Behind a lot of big stories there's somebody who isn't on stage. Yesterday's telling of Akiva's beginning, the man and the stone, comes from Avot de-Rabbi Natan. The Talmud tells it another way: through the woman who believed in him before anyone else did.
screen: `THE ACCEPTANCE SPEECH.` → `SOMEONE NOT ON STAGE.` → `THE WOMAN BEHIND AKIVA.`

segments.voice: In tractate Ketubot, Akiva is a shepherd working for Kalba Savua, a very rich man. The rich man's daughter sees something in him: he's modest and good. She asks: if I marry you, will you go and study? He says yes. They marry quietly, and her father, furious, cuts her off without a penny. Tradition knows her as Rachel. Akiva goes away to study for twelve years. Coming home, he hears an old man mocking her outside the house: how long will you live like a widow with a living husband? And she answers: if he listened to me, he'd stay away another twelve. So he turns around, without even going in, and studies twelve more. When he finally returns, twenty-four thousand students walk with him. His wife goes out to meet him and falls at his feet. The students don't know who she is, and start to push her away. Akiva stops them. Leave her, he says. What is mine and what is yours is hers. Everything I know, and everything I've taught you, belongs to her. Parts of this story are hard to hear today: years apart, poverty, a father's anger. The Talmud doesn't hide them. But its last word is gratitude, said out loud, in front of everyone.

Let one face come, and stay with them. If you had the microphone, what would you say?

277.title: Honi draws a circle (Taanit 23a)
277.hook: in drought, Honi draws a circle and won't step out until it rains
277.howItsDone: Jewish prayer includes asking for rain in its season; from late fall until Passover a line for rain is added to the daily Amidah, and stories like Honi's are told about bold, personal prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rachel, and Akiva telling his students that everything he had was hers. Your line was what is mine is hers.

Requests usually come padded. If it's not too much trouble. Only if you have time. Totally fine if not. People shrink their requests so no one has to say no. Now picture a dry land in late winter. The rains haven't come. Fields are cracking, cisterns are empty, and the people go to one man, known for his prayers: pray for rain. He does. Nothing happens. So he draws a circle in the dirt around himself. Today, Honi, and a prayer that was anything but polite.
screen: `ONLY IF IT'S NO TROUBLE.` → `A LAND WITHOUT RAIN.` → `A CIRCLE IN THE DIRT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Mishnah and the Talmud, tractate Taanit. Honi stands inside his circle and speaks to God. Master of the world, your children have turned to me, because I'm like a member of your household. I swear by your great name, I won't move from this circle until you have mercy on your children. A few drops fall. Honi says: that's not what I asked for. I asked for rain to fill the cisterns and the pits and the caves. Now it pours, violent and frightening. Not that either, says Honi. I asked for rain of goodwill, of blessing, of generosity. Then it rains the right way, steadily, until the people have to climb the Temple Mount to get out of the water, and they ask him to pray for it to stop. The name stuck: Honi the circle-drawer. The great sage of the time, Shimon ben Shetach, sent him a message half scolding, half wonder. If you weren't Honi, I'd put you under a ban. But what can I do? You nag God like a child nagging his father, and his father gives him what he wants. That's the heart of it. Honi isn't bargaining like a stranger. He's asking like family, boldly and specifically, and not taking drizzle for an answer.

segments.voice: Picture a circle drawn around where you sit, and inside it name one thing you really want, for yourself or for someone else: not the polite version, the real, specific one, this person healing, this debt paid, this friendship mended. If you pray, you can ask for it the way Honi did, like family; if not, simply say it clearly inside yourself and stay in the circle with it.
Honi, known ever after as the circle-drawer. In a drought he drew a circle, refused to step out until rain came, and then asked for the right rain.
Your line: draw the circle. Honi stayed in his circle until the right rain came. That's day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: The carob tree (Taanit 23a)
278.hook: an old man plants a tree he'll never eat from, for his grandchildren
278.howItsDone: The carob story is often told on Tu BiShvat, the new year of trees, when some Jews plant trees or eat fruits such as carob.

segments.voice: Yesterday Honi drew a circle and wouldn't step out until the rain came. Your line was draw the circle.

Somebody planted the big tree on your street. Somebody dug the well, laid the stones of the oldest building in town, started the library, wrote down the recipe your family still makes. Most of them never knew your name. They did the work and left it for whoever came next. The Talmud tells of Honi, the circle-drawer, walking down a road and meeting one of those people: a man, planting a tree.
screen: `WHO PLANTED YOUR STREET'S TREE?` → `THEY NEVER KNEW YOUR NAME.` → `A MAN, PLANTING.`

segments.voice: It's the same page of tractate Taanit as yesterday's circle. You met this scene once before, with Rabbi Tarfon, as a picture of work you won't finish. Today, look closer. Honi sees a man planting a carob tree. Retellings usually make him old; the Talmud just says a certain man. Honi asks: how long until this tree gives fruit? Seventy years, the man says. Honi presses: are you sure you'll live another seventy years? Listen to the order of the answer. He doesn't start with the future. He starts with what he found. I found the world with carob trees in it. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I'm planting for my children. First he notices a gift. Then he passes it on. The planting grows out of the noticing. In the Psalms, seventy years is a full life, so he's planting past the edge of his own, on purpose. The story keeps going, and Honi's next seventy years will surprise him. More on that soon. For today, stay with the word found. It's a small picture of how a tradition works at all. Every teaching on this path, somebody planted. They memorized it, copied it, argued over it, carried it through exile, and passed it down to people they'd never meet. Including you.

Then think of one small thing you could start that someone will enjoy after you: a seed in a pot, a note in a book, a family recipe taught to a kid.

279.title: This too is for good (Taanit 21a)
279.hook: Nachum of Gamzu met every setback by saying this too is for good
279.howItsDone: Gam zu l'tovah is an everyday Jewish expression, said when plans fall through; a related saying in the Talmud, attributed to Rabbi Akiva, is that everything the Merciful One does is for good.

segments.voice: Yesterday a man planted a carob tree, because his ancestors had planted for him. Your line was plant for others.

You miss the train. The coffee spills. The email you were waiting for says no. There's a split second before you react when you get to decide what this is. A disaster? An annoyance? A story you'll tell later? One sage in the Talmud filled that split second with the same three Hebrew words, every single time. Gam zu l'tovah. This too is for good. People called him Nachum Ish Gam Zu: Nachum, the this-too man.
screen: `THE TRAIN, THE COFFEE, THE NO.` → `A SPLIT SECOND TO DECIDE.` → `NACHUM, THE THIS-TOO MAN.`

segments.voice: Tractate Taanit tells it. The Jewish community wanted to send a gift to the emperor in Rome, and chose Nachum to carry it, because miracles seemed to follow him. They gave him a chest full of jewels. On the way he stopped at an inn, and in the night the innkeepers opened the chest, stole the jewels, and filled it with dirt. In the morning Nachum saw what had happened, and said: this too is for good. At the palace he opened the chest before the emperor. Dirt. The emperor was furious and ordered him killed. Then the story turns. A stranger appeared among the emperor's advisers; the Talmud says it was the prophet Elijah. Maybe, he said, this is the dirt of their ancestor Abraham, who threw dust that turned into swords. The Romans tried it against a province they had never managed to conquer, and it worked. Nachum went home honored, his chest full of treasure. One careful point. The same passage says Nachum lived with great suffering: he was blind, with no hands or feet, and his body was covered in sores. So his three words weren't a smile pasted over pain. They were a way of trusting that the story isn't finished yet. Nachum doesn't say this is good. He says this, too, is for good. The word for does a lot of work.

280.title: It is not in heaven (Bava Metzia 59b)
280.hook: a heavenly voice backs Rabbi Eliezer, and the sages answer: the Torah is not in heaven (Deuteronomy 30:12)
280.howItsDone: Jewish law is decided by reasoned argument among scholars, following rules such as the majority view, and the story of the oven of Akhnai is often used to teach this.

segments.voice: Yesterday Nachum met every setback with gam zu l'tovah. Your line was this too for the good.

If I'm right, let that tree prove it. One rabbi says that in the middle of an argument, and the tree pulls itself out of the ground and moves a hundred cubits. Most arguments would end right there. In the Talmud, it didn't work. The question was a small legal one: could a certain kind of clay oven become ritually impure? Rabbi Eliezer said one thing. Everyone else said another. What happened next is today's story.
screen: `IF I'M RIGHT, LET THE TREE PROVE IT.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT AN OVEN.` → `ONE AGAINST ALL.`

segments.voice: In tractate Bava Metzia, Rabbi Eliezer brings every argument in the world, and the sages don't accept them. So he says: if the law is as I say, let this carob tree prove it. The tree uproots itself. The sages answer: you don't bring proof from a carob tree. Let the stream prove it. The water flows backward. You don't bring proof from a stream. Let the walls of the study house prove it. The walls begin to lean. Rabbi Yehoshua scolds the walls: when scholars argue, what business is it of yours? So they don't fall, out of respect for Rabbi Yehoshua, and they don't straighten, out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer. The Talmud says they're still leaning. Finally a voice comes from heaven: why do you argue with Rabbi Eliezer? The law is like him everywhere. Rabbi Yehoshua stands and quotes the Torah: "It is not in heaven." In Deuteronomy, those words are Moses telling the people the teaching isn't far away or up in the sky; it's close, in your mouth and in your heart. Another sage explains: the Torah was already given at Sinai. We don't decide law by voices from heaven. The Torah itself, as the rabbis read it, says to follow the majority. That's a startling move. The sages take the Torah so seriously that they refuse a miracle. Once the teaching is given, it's in human hands, to be argued, reasoned and decided here on earth.
screen: `THE TREE, THE STREAM, THE WALLS.` · `A VOICE FROM HEAVEN.` · `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.` · `NOW IT'S IN HUMAN HANDS.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: First, a look back at this week: Hillel on the roof, water wearing stone, Akiva and Rachel, Honi's circle, the carob tree, gam zu l'tovah. Now pick one question you've been waiting for someone else to answer, a decision, a belief, a hard choice, and instead of waiting for a sign, think it through yourself for one minute. What do you know, what would a wise friend say, and what's close, in your own mouth and heart?
Rabbi Yehoshua, who answered a heavenly voice with words from Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. The Torah was given, and now it's ours to reason through.
Your line: ours to reason through. The teaching is close, not up in the sky. Two hundred eighty days now.

chat.says: A heavenly voice sided with Rabbi Eliezer, so why didn't the sages give in?
options: Because the Torah is not in heaven; it was given, ours to reason out.
They doubted the voice was real, so they simply ignored it.
They thought Rabbi Eliezer had faked the miracles to win.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Yehoshua quoted Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. The Torah was given at Sinai; law is decided here, by reasoning and the majority.
